title: How Much Faster Does AI Actually Make Programmers?

sentences.text: How much faster does AI actually make the people who write code?
Ask around and the answers point in opposite directions, from enormous multiples to slower than before.
sentences.note: Frames the two attributed claims in s04 and s05; carries no figure.

sentences.text: So set the loudest answers aside, look at the studies that measured programmers at work, and ask what each one actually measured.

sections.name: question-1
sections.title: How much faster does AI make programmers?

sentences.text: On the Lex Fridman Podcast, DHH described "that magical 10X, 100X, in a few rare cases, 1000X productivity boost", and said that to get it you have to work with the AI agents directly.

assertions.text: DHH, on the Lex Fridman Podcast, said that getting a 10X, 100X or in rare cases 1000X productivity boost requires interacting with the agents directly.

quote.text: that magical 10X, 100X, in a few rare cases, 1000X productivity boost
quote.speaker: DHH

sentences.text: From the other side, a run of videos and posts repeats one trial's result, in the words of the channel Macro Lens: when experienced developers were allowed AI tools, "they were 19% slower than when they weren't".

assertions.text: Several videos and posts report that experienced developers were 19% slower with AI tools.
The channel Macro Lens said that when the developers were allowed AI tools they were 19% slower than when they weren't.

quote.text: they were 19% slower than when they weren't
quote.speaker: Macro Lens

sentences.text: Start with ordinary workplaces.

One set of field experiments followed almost five thousand software developers at three companies, in their regular jobs and partly over years, and estimated that an AI code suggestion tool raised their productivity, measured by their output, by about 26 percent.

assertions.text: Observing the output of almost 5000 software developers at three companies in their regular jobs, partly over years, the authors estimate that a generative AI code suggestion tool raised developer productivity by 26.08%, about 26%.
qualifications: s11 to s14 give the METR trial, where experienced developers in large, mature open-source projects were slowed, and the researchers' hypothesis that project size and complexity explain it.

sentences.text: The authors note that this is substantially smaller than an earlier lab result, and suggest why: some kinds of coding are less readily helped by the tool, and coding is only part of a developer's job.

assertions.text: The field estimate is substantially smaller than the lab result of Peng et al.; the authors suggest some coding tasks are less readily assisted by the tool and coding is only part of a developer's job.
qualifications: s11 to s14 give the METR trial, where experienced developers in large, mature open-source projects were slowed, and the researchers' hypothesis that project size and complexity explain it.

sentences.text: A separate trial estimated a roughly 21 percent increase in development speed attributable to AI, but that estimate missed the usual bar for statistical significance, so it is less certain than it sounds.

assertions.text: The trial estimated a roughly 21% increase in development speed attributable to AI in its best-fit model, an effect that did not meet the usual significance threshold.
qualifications: s09 says the estimate did not reach statistical significance.

sentences.text: Then there is the trial behind those slowdown claims.

METR ran a randomized controlled trial with 16 experienced open-source developers on 246 tasks in mature projects they had worked on for an average of 5 years, randomly allowing or disallowing AI tools task by task.

assertions.text: METR's randomized controlled trial had 16 experienced open-source developers complete 246 tasks in mature projects on which they had an average of 5 years of prior experience, with each task randomly assigned to allow or disallow AI tools.

sentences.text: The tools were the February to June 2025 frontier: mostly the Cursor Pro editor with Claude 3.5 and 3.7 Sonnet.

assertions.text: The trial tested AI tools at the February-June 2025 frontier; developers primarily used Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet.

sentences.text: With AI allowed, tasks took 19 percent longer to complete.

assertions.text: Allowing AI increased task completion time by 19%.
qualifications: s11 and s12 give the population, the projects and the early-2025 tools beside this figure.

sentences.text: The researchers' hypothesis for why AI helped less than in earlier trials: their projects averaged about 10 years old and more than 1,100,000 lines of code, compared with the more greenfield projects in those trials.

assertions.text: METR hypothesizes that AI helped its developers less than in earlier RCTs because of the size and complexity of the repositories, which average about 10 years old and >1,100,000 lines of code, compared with the more greenfield projects in Peng et al. and other trials.
qualifications: s14 presents it as the researchers' hypothesis, not a finding.
s14 says these are open-source projects in METR's trial, not workplace codebases (s11).

sentences.text: But would newer tools change that?
METR's own 2026 update says that, from talking to participants, it believes developers are likely more sped up in early 2026 than in early 2025.

assertions.text: Based on conversations with study participants, METR believes it is likely that developers are more sped up from AI tools in early 2026 than in its early 2025 estimates.
qualifications: s18 says METR calls its new data only very weak evidence because of selection effects.
s18 says METR calls the new data only very weak evidence because of selection effects.

sentences.text: Its new raw numbers lean the same way: tasks took an estimated 18 percent less time for returning developers and 4 percent less for new recruits, but both ranges still stretch to a slowdown.

assertions.text: METR's later study estimates a speedup of -18% (confidence interval -38% to +9%) for returning developers and -4% (confidence interval -15% to +9%) for newly recruited developers; both intervals reach into longer task times.
qualifications: s17 says both ranges include a slowdown; s18 gives the selection problem.
s18 says METR calls the new data only very weak evidence because of selection effects.

sentences.note: In METR's convention a negative speedup is a reduction in completion time (the early-2025 result is +19% time, CI +2% to +39%), so -18% is 18% less time and the +9% upper bounds are longer times.

sentences.text: And METR calls this only very weak evidence: more developers now decline to take part because they don't want to work without AI, which likely pushes its speedup estimate down, so the ones left are not a fair sample.

assertions.text: Because of the selection effects in its new experiment, METR calls its data only very weak evidence for the size of the increase in speedup.
qualifications: s18 is itself the qualification: METR calls the new data only very weak evidence because of selection effects.

assertions.text: METR observed a significant increase in developers choosing not to participate in its new experiment because they do not wish to work without AI, which it says likely biases its estimate of AI-assisted speedup downwards.

sentences.note: The participation clause is METR's own reason (L60 of the update, inside the L58-L62 verdict passage s11 also cites); the very-weak-evidence clause is L61.

sentences.text: And the multiples from the start?

The largest figures so far come from Anthropic's own report on its staff: employees self-reported that they now get a 50 percent productivity gain from Claude on average, and merged pull requests per engineer per day rose 67 percent when its engineering org adopted Claude Code.

assertions.text: Anthropic employees self-reported that they now use Claude in 59% of their work and get +50% productivity gains from it on average.
qualifications: s20 says the 50 percent is self-reported.
s20 says the 50 percent is self-reported and s21 that the 67 percent counts merged changes, not time saved; both are one company's report on its own staff.

assertions.text: Anthropic saw a 67% increase in merged pull requests per engineer per day when it adopted Claude Code across its engineering org.
qualifications: s20 says the 50 percent is self-reported and s21 that the 67 percent counts merged changes, not time saved; both are one company's report on its own staff.

sentences.text: A count of merged changes is not the same as time saved, but even taken at face value, both figures are an order of magnitude below ten times.

assertions.text: A self-reported +50% gain and 67% more merged pull requests are an order of magnitude below 10x.
qualifications: s20 says the 50 percent is self-reported and s21 that the 67 percent counts merged changes, not time saved; both are one company's report on its own staff.

sentences.note: 'A count of merged changes is not time saved' names what the 67 percent measures: the passage defines merged pull requests as successfully incorporated changes to code.

sentences.text: So, how much faster? In the workplace studies, with the tools they tested, the measured gains were modest, nowhere near the multiples in the hype.

assertions.text: Field and trial estimates in workplaces with the assistants they tested (26.08% more output; a roughly 21% speed increase that missed significance) show modest average gains, far below headline claims.
qualifications: s09 says the second estimate missed statistical significance; s23 gives the exception for experienced developers in mature projects.
s11 to s14 give the METR trial, where experienced developers in large, mature open-source projects were slowed, and the researchers' hypothesis that project size and complexity explain it.

sentences.text: For experienced developers in big, mature projects they knew well, early-2025 tools made them slower, and whether today's tools have reversed that, METR's own newer data is too weak to say.

assertions.text: Early-2025 AI tools increased completion time for experienced open-source developers on mature projects they knew well.
METR's newer data is only very weak evidence for how much developers are sped up now, because of selection effects.
qualifications: s23 says the newer data cannot settle it.
s18 says METR calls the new data only very weak evidence because of selection effects.

sentences.text: But that slowdown trial holds a stranger detail, and it is about what the developers believed was happening.

sections.name: question-2
sections.title: Can developers tell whether AI is speeding them up?

sentences.text: Take a second and make your own guess: how much time does AI save you?
Before starting, the METR developers forecast that allowing AI would cut their completion time by 24 percent.

assertions.text: Before starting tasks, the developers forecast that allowing AI would reduce completion time by 24%.
qualifications: s30 gives the Copilot trial, where participants underestimated a 55.8 percent gain, so overestimation is not stated as the rule.

sentences.text: After the study, with the work behind them, they estimated it had cut their time by 20 percent, in the same trial that measured them taking longer.

assertions.text: After completing the study, the developers estimated that allowing AI had reduced completion time by 20%, while the trial found it increased completion time.
qualifications: s30 gives the Copilot trial, where participants underestimated a 55.8 percent gain, so overestimation is not stated as the rule.

sentences.text: Outside experts did no better: economists predicted 39 percent shorter completion times, and machine learning experts 38 percent.

assertions.text: Experts in economics predicted 39% shorter completion times and experts in ML predicted 38% shorter.
qualifications: s30 gives the Copilot trial, where participants underestimated a 55.8 percent gain, so overestimation is not stated as the rule.

sentences.text: So people overestimate the gain? Not always.

In an earlier randomized trial of Copilot, a lab task on a greenfield-style project, the measured productivity gain was 55.8 percent, yet participants in both the AI and the control group estimated 35 percent on average: they underestimated it.

assertions.text: In the Copilot trial, participants in both treated and control groups estimated a 35% increase in productivity on average, an underestimation compared with the 55.8% increase in their revealed productivity.
qualifications: s26 to s28 give the METR trial, where developers and experts overestimated.

assertions.text: Peng et al.'s Copilot result came from a software engineering task in the lab, on a more greenfield project.
qualifications: s30 names it as a lab task on a greenfield-style project.

sentences.text: So the same kind of guess missed in opposite directions: too high for experienced developers in big projects they knew well, too low on a fresh task in the lab.

assertions.text: METR's experienced developers on their mature projects overestimated their speedup, while participants in the Copilot lab trial underestimated theirs.
qualifications: s31 presents both trials, one overestimate and one underestimate, so neither is stated as the rule.
s30 gives the Copilot trial, where participants underestimated a 55.8 percent gain, so overestimation is not stated as the rule.

sentences.text: METR's later update adds that some developers now self-report very high speedups, and repeats that, as its earlier study found, such estimates can be quite unreliable.

assertions.text: METR's later update says some developers self-report very high speedups, and that as its earlier study documented those estimates can be quite unreliable.
qualifications: s30 gives the Copilot trial, where participants underestimated their gain.

sentences.text: So can developers tell? In both of these trials, not reliably: their guesses missed by a wide margin.

assertions.text: In METR's trial developers' estimates were far above the measured effect, and in the Copilot trial participants' estimates were far below it.
qualifications: s30 gives the Copilot trial, where participants underestimated a 55.8 percent gain, so overestimation is not stated as the rule.

sentences.text: Every number in this video belongs to particular people, doing particular work, with particular tools.

So when someone tells you how much faster AI makes them, ask what they measured, and if you want to know for yourself, time comparable tasks with the tool and without it rather than trusting the feeling.
